source: de Vivo et al. (2017) Ultrastructural evidence for synaptic scaling across the wake/sleep cycle
finding: 3D electron microscopy of mouse cortex found synapses are smaller after sleep than after wake. The shrinkage was proportional to size (scaling) but selective: large synapses were spared.
numbers: 6,920 synapses, 168 dendritic segments, 3 groups x 4 mice (sleep, spontaneous wake, enforced wake), layer 2 of M1 and S1. Axon-spine interface (ASI) 18.9% smaller vs spontaneous wake (p=0.001) and 17.5% vs enforced wake (p=0.003). Wake groups did not differ (-1.7%, p=0.957). Best model: >80% of synapses scale, <20% (largest) do not. Small-medium synapses -11.9% / -12.5%; large +0.7% / +2.0%. Only spines with endosome-like vesicles/tubules scaled (-25.0% / -20.9%); spines without them -2.9% / -2.8%.
quote: Scaling was selective, sparing synapses that were large and lacked recycling endosomes.
limits: Only 4 mice per group; one cortical layer; ASI is a structural proxy for strength; a snapshot at the end of wake or sleep, not a within-animal change. Sleep effect largest in sparsely spiny dendrites (-36.4% vs -7.8% at high density).
agent_relevance: Do not shrink everything. Down-select by size/strength and by recent plasticity: strong, stable lessons are protected; weak and recently touched ones are pruned.

source: Diering et al. (2017) Homer1a drives homeostatic scaling-down of excitatory synapses during sleep
finding: In mice, synaptic AMPA receptors (GluA1) and their phosphorylation fall during sleep. This needs Homer1a and mGluR1/5 signalling, and is driven by noradrenaline (wake) and adenosine (sleep need).
numbers: PSD fractions N=8 brains per condition. Proteomics: >4,500 PSD proteins and ~10,000 phosphopeptides measured; ~20% of PSD proteins/sites changed between wake and sleep. In vivo two-photon: 383 spines from 4 mice; spines with high wake GluA1 (n=168) dropped more than low-GluA1 spines (n=215); more spines fell than rose (KS test p<0.05).
limits: Mouse biochemistry; few animals for imaging; Homer1a knockout changes other things, so the causal story is indirect.
agent_relevance: Strongest items lose the most, and the process runs only when the system is offline (no input). A rule that could be copied: prune when not serving a task.

source: Bushey, Tononi, Cirelli (2011) Sleep and synaptic homeostasis: structural evidence in Drosophila
finding: In three fly circuits, synapse size or number rises after wake and falls only if the fly sleeps. Richer waking experience gave bigger synaptic growth and more sleep need. The Fmr1 gene is needed for the renormalization.
numbers: Presynaptic puncta width measured in S (n=34), SD (n=26), W (n=20) groups; VS1 spine counts rose after sleep deprivation, mainly stubby spines; mushroom spines unchanged (p=0.29). Fmr1-overexpressing flies slept 9.6% less (WT n=110, OE n=62, p<0.05) and recovered 39% of lost sleep vs 49% for WT (p<0.05).
limits: Flies, not mammals; mechanisms may differ. Counts of spines and puncta, not synaptic strength. The wake-experience link to sleep need is partly correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports the 'why prune at all' argument: growth during activity is the default and needs a scheduled offline reduction.

source: Tononi and Cirelli (2012) Time to be SHY? Some comments on sleep and synaptic homeostasis
finding: Reply to Frank's critique. States that SHY is about the function of sleep (restoring synaptic homeostasis), not about one mechanism. Argues slow-wave activity (SWA) is a good sensor of synaptic strength but concedes evidence that SWA acts as the effector of downscaling is limited and indirect.
numbers: Example: visual deprivation in the critical period cut SWA by 40% in mice and cats. In rats, the slope of local field potentials at end of wake correlates with SWA at sleep onset.
quote: so far the evidence supporting it remains limited and indirect
limits: Authors' own defence, not neutral. The theory was narrowed to 'function, not mechanism' after criticism, which weakens how falsifiable it is.
agent_relevance: Separate the function (keep the store bounded and useful) from the mechanism (which operator does it). Specify what prune must achieve, not one fixed recipe.

source: Frank (2012) Erasing synapses in sleep: is it time to be SHY?
finding: Main critique: SHY is elegant, but the cellular mechanism is unclear and its functional significance unknown. Raises brain temperature and glucocorticoids as alternative explanations (as seen in the Tononi-Cirelli reply).
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers.
limits: Abstract read, full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat 'sleep prunes' as a design hypothesis, not a settled fact.

source: Aton et al. (2014) Sleep promotes cortical response potentiation following visual experience
finding: Rival result: in adult mouse visual cortex, response potentiation after patterned visual experience occurred only after sleep and was blocked by sleep deprivation. Potentiation scaled with phase-locking to spindles.
numbers: Abstract only: V1 neurons recorded before and after an oriented grating, then sleep or sleep deprivation; sample size not read.
limits: Abstract only. Contradicts a blanket 'sleep only weakens' view, so SHY must allow selective strengthening.
agent_relevance: A good pruning step also strengthens the right lessons. Do not make prune one-directional.

source: Yang et al. (2014) Sleep promotes branch-specific formation of dendritic spines after learning
finding: After motor learning, sleep promotes new spines on a subset of dendritic branches. NREM reactivation of learning-activated neurons is needed. Sleep deprivation cuts learning-induced spine formation.
numbers: 24 h after training, spine formation on high-formation branches was 15.3 +/- 1.3% vs 6.4 +/- 0.8% (untrained high) and 4.4 +/- 0.9% (untrained low), p<0.0001; only ~30% of branches responded. Sleep deprivation (7 h): awake 97.0 +/- 2.1% vs 26.4 +/- 2.9% in controls; learning-induced spine formation reduced.
limits: Spine formation is structural, not strength. It shows sleep can add as well as remove, which does not contradict net renormalization but limits the 'sleep = delete' reading.
agent_relevance: Counter-pressure to pure pruning: replayed items get consolidated into new protected structure. Keep prune and promote together.

source: Zhou et al. (2020) REM sleep promotes experience-dependent dendritic spine elimination in the mouse cortex
finding: Elimination of spines after monocular deprivation or fear conditioning was reduced by total sleep or REM sleep deprivation; REM dendritic calcium spikes were needed.
numbers: Abstract only: 1-month-old mice, layer 5 pyramidal neurons in V1 and frontal association cortex.
limits: Abstract only. Shows pruning can be experience-specific and REM-driven, not global NREM downscaling.
agent_relevance: Prune what was recently used or contradicted, not everything.

source: Torrado Pacheco et al. (2021) Sleep promotes downward firing rate homeostasis
finding: After an activity boost (eye reopening after monocular deprivation), V1 firing overshot, then returned to each neuron's set point. The downward return happened during sleep, not wake, and was slower when sleep was reduced.
numbers: Firing of reopened-hemisphere neurons rose 114 +/- 23% from baseline on ER2 and was back to 2 +/- 13% by ER4 (controls 10 +/- 18%); 30 of 36 neurons (83.3%) rose then fell. Hebbian firing depression happened regardless of sleep or wake.
limits: Rat V1 perturbation paradigm, not natural learning. Intermittent sleep deprivation slowed but did not abolish the return.
agent_relevance: Upward corrections can happen online; downward correction is best scheduled offline. In the agent: add lessons online, prune in a separate pass.

source: Hengen et al. (2016) Neuronal firing rate homeostasis is inhibited by sleep and promoted by wake
finding: Opposite direction: after visual deprivation, V1 firing recovered to its set point during active wake and was suppressed during sleep.
numbers: Abstract only; rats, visual cortex.
limits: Abstract read only. Torrado Pacheco 2021 reconciles it as upward homeostasis in wake and downward in sleep. An earlier Hengen 2013 paper found the rebound independent of sleep-wake state.
agent_relevance: Be careful: 'sleep does homeostasis' is direction-specific.

source: Vyazovskiy et al. (2009) Cortical firing and sleep homeostasis
finding: In rats, after sustained wake cortical neurons fired faster in all states; after sustained sleep firing rate and synchrony fell. Changes in NREM firing tracked slow-wave activity.
numbers: Abstract only: sample size not read.
limits: Abstract only. SHY says the regulated variable is synaptic strength, not firing rate, so this is indirect support.
agent_relevance: A measurable 'pressure to prune' exists in brains (SWA). The agent can use store size or redundancy as its own pressure signal.

source: Watson et al. (2016) Network homeostasis and state dynamics of neocortical sleep
finding: Challenge: in rat frontal cortex, NREM lowered firing of fast-firing neurons but raised firing of slow-firing ones; REM lowered firing across the range. Net effect: the firing-rate distribution became more uniform, 'at variance with current homeostatic models'.
numbers: Abstract only: large-scale recordings in rats.
limits: Abstract only. Not a refutation of synaptic downscaling (rates are not synapses) but a rival: sleep homogenizes, it does not simply shrink.
agent_relevance: A 'homogenize' operator (rescue weak items, trim dominant ones) is a candidate alternative to uniform decay.

source: Cary and Turrigiano (2021) Stability of neocortical synapses across sleep and wake states during the critical period in rats
finding: Failed to find sleep-driven downscaling in juvenile rat cortex: miniature EPSC amplitudes in L4 and L2/3 of V1 and PFC were stable across sleep- and wake-dense periods; thalamocortical efficacy was stable over prolonged natural sleep and wake.
numbers: Abstract only: sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Critical-period animals; authors say generalization to the mature brain is unknown. de Vivo 2019 found the opposite in 2-week-old mice with ASI (different species and measure).
agent_relevance: Pruning may not be universal; it may matter once a lot of mature content has accumulated.

source: de Vivo et al. (2019) Evidence for sleep-dependent synaptic renormalization in mouse pups
finding: In 2-week-old mouse pups, motor-cortex layer 2 synapses were smaller after sleep than after extended wake, consistent with multiplicative scaling.
numbers: ASI 33.9% smaller after sleep relative to extended wake. Pups sleep ~50% of the day. Two strains (CD-1, YFP-H); SBEM in YFP-H pups.
limits: One layer in one area; same lab as the 2017 paper. Conflicts with Cary and Turrigiano (2021) in juveniles.
agent_relevance: Renormalization may be needed even while the system is still growing, so a new agent may need pruning too.

source: Spano et al. (2019) Sleep deprivation by exposure to novel objects increases synapse density and axon-spine interface in hippocampal CA1
finding: Extends the SBEM result to hippocampus CA1: ASI sizes grew after wake, more after enforced wake, and synapse density also rose after enforced wake.
numbers: Abstract only: sleep n=6, spontaneous wake n=4, enforced wake n=4 adolescent mice; ~425 ASIs per animal; ~100 synapses per mouse for vesicle counts. Readily available vesicle proportion fell after enforced wake.
limits: Abstract only. Contrast: Havekes 2016 found 5 h of sleep deprivation cut CA1 spine numbers.
agent_relevance: The fast-store analogue (raw episode log) also needs pruning.

source: Havekes et al. (2016) Sleep deprivation causes memory deficits by negatively impacting neuronal connectivity in hippocampal area CA1
finding: Opposite direction in hippocampus: 5 h of sleep deprivation decreased dendritic spine numbers in CA1 (cofilin activity up via PDE4A5); recovery sleep normalized them.
numbers: Abstract only: mice; 5 h gentle-handling sleep deprivation.
limits: Abstract only. Differs from Spano 2019 in method (gentle handling vs novel objects) and measure (spine number vs ASI size); not reconciled.
agent_relevance: How the system is kept 'awake' (extra stimulation vs plain staying up) changed the result.

source: Bridi et al. (2020) Daily oscillation of the excitation-inhibition balance in visual cortical circuits
finding: Synaptic inhibition in visual cortex goes up during the light (sleep) phase, opposite to excitation, in a sleep-dependent way. So down-selection is not only excitatory weakening: the E/I balance shifts too.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Pruning can also be done by adding a veto or filter at retrieval, not only by deleting entries.

source: Gonzalez-Rueda et al. (2018) Activity-dependent downscaling of subthreshold synaptic inputs during slow-wave-sleep-like activity in vivo
finding: In anesthetized mice with SWS-like activity, Up states bias toward depression: presynaptic stimulation alone weakens a synapse, but connections that contribute to postsynaptic spiking are protected.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; anesthetized (urethane) preparation.
agent_relevance: A concrete selection rule: decay what fires without contributing, protect what contributed to an outcome. Maps to 'prune lessons that were retrieved but never helped'.

source: Kuhn et al. (2016) Sleep recalibrates homeostatic and associative synaptic plasticity in the human cortex
finding: In humans, one night of sleep deprivation raised markers of net synaptic strength (lower TMS intensity needed, higher EEG theta) and reduced LTP-like plasticity and memory formation. Plasma BDNF is a candidate mechanism.
numbers: N=20, within-subject, counterbalanced sleep vs sleep deprivation, one-week gap. PAS rm-ANOVA: Condition F(1,19)=7.5, p=0.013, partial eta2=0.283; Condition x Time F(3,57)=3.5, p=0.021, partial eta2=0.156. Post 2: LTP-like rise after sleep t(19)=2.6, p=0.018; fall after deprivation t(19)=-2.8, p=0.013. TMS intensity lower after deprivation t(19)=-2.46, p=0.023.
limits: N=20, indirect non-invasive indices, motor cortex only; no independent replication read this session.
agent_relevance: Cost of skipping the offline pass: less ability to take in new items (saturation). Testable in the agent: does a memory with no pruning learn new lessons worse?

source: Tononi and Cirelli (2020) Sleep and synaptic down-selection
finding: Updated review. Argues down-selection is driven by cortical slow-wave Up states and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples, and cites ASI shrinkage and AMPA receptor loss. Says SHY allows some depression in wake and some potentiation in sleep, because only the net change is claimed; disputes contrary readings by Puentes-Mestril and Aton (2017) and Frank and Seibt (2018).
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Authors' own review. The disagreements are stated, not tested.
agent_relevance: Down-selection can be cued by replay: entries replayed and found useful are protected.

source: Cirelli and Tononi (2022) The why and how of sleep-dependent synaptic down-selection
finding: Recent review. In cortex and hippocampus the spread between low and high firing cells falls in NREM and rises in REM, but the effects cancel to an overall decrease. The trigger is not a change in mean firing rate. Authors admit firing data cannot separate NREM and REM contributions.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Review by the theory's authors. Firing-rate changes may reflect excitability rather than synaptic strength.
agent_relevance: Two phases with opposite biases and a net reduction: a prune pass plus a rebuild/refresh pass.

source: Tadros et al. (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks
finding: Not an LLM. In small neural networks, a sleep phase of local Hebbian learning with noisy input recovered old tasks. But a stored 0.75% rehearsal buffer beat sleep alone on most benchmarks.
numbers: Test accuracy (%): incremental MNIST sequential 19.49, sleep (SRC) 48.47, rehearsal 0.75% 79.91, rehearsal+SRC 86.47, OWM 77.04, parallel ideal 98.02. Multi-modal MNIST: sequential 47.18, SRC 61.33, parallel 90.05. Incremental CIFAR10: SRC 44.55, rehearsal 39.39, rehearsal+SRC 58.24.
limits: Small image tasks, 5 benchmark columns; SRC alone loses to OWM and to rehearsal on incremental MNIST and Fashion MNIST.
agent_relevance: Sleep-like phases help most when combined with a small replay buffer; keep a few raw cases when consolidating.

source: Capone et al. (2019) Sleep-like slow oscillations improve visual classification through synaptic homeostasis and memory association in a thalamo-cortical model
finding: In a thalamo-cortical spiking model trained on MNIST digits, deep-sleep-like slow oscillations with STDP produced a selective homeostatic weight change and memory association, and raised classification accuracy over the sleep period.
numbers: Test set of 250 images per trial; 3 training examples per digit (30 total). Accuracy rose across 3000 s of sleep; the exact gain could not be read from the extracted text.
limits: Spiking model with a tiny training set; gain figure not read exactly.
agent_relevance: Offline renormalization can help when data are few and noisy; a hint for few-shot lessons.

source: Robinson et al. (2022) Continual learning benefits from multiple sleep mechanisms: NREM, REM, and synaptic downscaling
finding: Not an LLM. In class-incremental CIFAR-100, adding synaptic downscaling (zero the smallest fraction p of weights before each task) on top of generative replay kept earlier tasks longer but cost new-task learning. Best near p=0.75.
numbers: p tested = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9; 10,000 Adam iterations per task. Without generative replay accuracy collapsed at every p. Maximum accuracy rose up to p=0.75 and fell at higher p; p<=0.5 looked like p=0.
limits: Read from text and figures; bootstrapped CIs; effect sizes not tabulated. 'Downscaling' here is magnitude pruning, a coarse stand-in.
agent_relevance: Trade-off: more aggressive pruning protects old lessons and hurts learning new ones. Moderate pruning, not extreme.

source: Massey et al. (2026) Sleep-based homeostatic regularization for stabilizing STDP in recurrent spiking neural networks
finding: Not an LLM. Periodic offline phases with noisy weight decay toward a baseline stabilized an STDP-trained spiking network, with an optimum at low to intermediate sleep. The same intervention gave no benefit in a gradient-trained spiking network.
numbers: Sleep 10-20% of training best for STDP-SNN; accuracy declines at higher sleep; 11 sleep levels (0% to 100%), 5 seeds, 4 MNIST-family datasets, beta-regression mixed model. SG-SNN (surrogate gradient): optimum at 0% sleep, net effect near zero.
limits: Small networks; the gradient-trained model had higher absolute accuracy anyway.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: decay helps a Hebbian runaway-growth learner but not a system with its own bounded optimizer. Check the store really runs away before adding prune.

source: Massey, Nichele, Hubin (2026) Exploring napping paradigm for recurrent spiking neural networks
finding: Not an LLM. Proportional weight scaling with noise matched the accuracy of weight normalization; accuracy peaked at brief naps and low noise, then fell monotonically with duration or noise. Decay toward a fixed target erodes relative structure.
numbers: Gabor-preprocessed MNIST; three regularization regimes; duration and noise sweeps. Strongest cluster separation at longer, noisier naps, but at lower accuracy.
limits: Single dataset; napping costs more simulation than normalization.
agent_relevance: Scale by ratio, not toward a fixed value: lower all weights but keep the relative ranking of lessons.

source: Shinde (2026) SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory with Algorithmic Forgetting for Large Language Models
finding: LLM memory prototype with sleep phases (Hebbian strengthening, synaptic downscaling, value-based pruning). On a self-built 8-test suite it kept all facts and removed most noise. The author calls it a research preview.
numbers: Ten-turn recall: FIFO 8/22 (36.4%), vector DB 19/22 (86.4%) with 55 concepts, no-forget graph 22/22 with 72 concepts, SCM 22/22 with 24 concepts. Noise removed 50/55 (90.9%). Ablation: no value tagger 18/22 (81.8%); no NREM consolidation 20/22 (90.9%); no forgetting module 22/22 but 72 concepts. A weight bug fix moved noise removal from 0% to 90.9% (beta 0.4 to 0.2).
limits: Tiny synthetic benchmark (22 facts, 50 noise items); weights chosen by ablation on the same suite; single author; no real-LLM downstream task or external benchmark.
agent_relevance: Pruning can cut store size with no loss on easy recall, but one hyperparameter swung the result from 0% to 90.9%. Test on real tasks.

source: Chauhan et al. (2026) Let Them Sleep: Recursive Self-Pruning Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
finding: Agent memory that sleeps every 10 tasks: clusters recent failures, distils each cluster to a rule, deletes the raw episodes, and decays rules unless reinforced. Gains in three settings, but pruning caused a large loss in one case.
numbers: SWE-bench simulation: solve rate 40.0% to 49.1% (+9.1 points, p=0.0003, 10 seeds); +5.4 points on easy issues, +13.2 on >4 h issues; 30.6% fewer entries. Temporal consistency 92.5% vs naive RAG 80.6%, oracle 88.4%, keyword detector 79.5% (12 benchmarks, 1,363 items). LoCoMo-10: 72.8%, +7.6 points (p=0.0042), 3,850 evaluations; memory flattened near 472 vs 675 entries. Failure case: one conversation with 35% error rate triggered 21 sleep cycles, pruned 43%, finished 19.5 points below baseline.
quote: a memory involved in a failure caused it
limits: Short paper; the SWE-bench part is a difficulty-calibrated simulation, not real agent runs; the ~93% fewer retry loops and ~30% less memory 'equilibrium' comes from separately tuned runs.
agent_relevance: Closest match to 'prune lessons'. The failure case gives a rule: do not delete memories merely because they were present in a failure. Gate pruning on the error rate.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: Sleep-inspired memory consolidation for resolving proactive interference in LLMs (SleepGate)
finding: A learned forgetting gate over the KV cache, triggered by attention entropy, evicts stale entries. On a synthetic proactive-interference benchmark with a 4-layer 793K-parameter transformer it beat all five baselines, with a cliff at depth 15.
numbers: N=200 episodes per depth, seven depths. SleepGate 99.5% (abstract: depth 5; body also gives depth 1), 97.0% at depth 10, 73.5% at depth 15, 16.5% at depth 30 (stale retrieval 62% at depth 30). All five baselines below 18% at all depths: full cache 8.0% at n=1, StreamingLLM 17.5%, decay-only ~12.5%. Sleep overhead 15.6%.
limits: Synthetic tokens (vocab 1024), toy transformer, no pre-trained model; transfer to real LLMs untested (the paper says so). Plain decay did no better than baselines.
agent_relevance: Plain decay is not enough; a content-aware gate that knows which entries were superseded is what works.

source: Wei et al. (2026) FadeMem: Biologically-inspired forgetting for efficient agent memory
finding: Adaptive exponential decay modulated by relevance, access frequency and time, plus LLM-guided fusion. Claims better retention than Mem0 and MemGPT at 45% less storage.
numbers: LTI-Bench 30 days: critical facts 82.1% (FadeMem) vs 78.4% (Mem0), 75.6% (MemGPT), 71.2% (LangChain), 50.2% (Fixed-16K); storage 55.0% vs 100% (Mem0). LoCoMo multi-hop F1 29.43 vs Mem0 28.37; MSC RP@10 77.2% vs 74.8%; storage reduction 0.45. Removing a component cut multi-hop F1 from 29.43 to 19.45 (-33.9%).
limits: Margin over Mem0 is small (about 1 F1 point; 2.4 points on MSC); LTI-Bench is the authors' own simulated benchmark; no repeated seeds or confidence intervals seen.
agent_relevance: Soft decay by use can match or beat keep-everything at about half the storage, but the margin over a good retriever is thin.

source: Kyrkewood (2026) The Sleeping Agent: what gist-based context compression loses and why
finding: Sleep-style gist compression of conversation history beats truncation on multi-hop and single-hop questions but loses dates and times, hurting temporal questions. One prompt sentence fixed most of it.
numbers: LoCoMo, ten conversations, 1,935 questions (1,501 in main analysis), temperature 0. Temporal-expression preservation 3.05% to 62.39% (about 20-fold); named entity and event preservation barely changed (x1.02, x1.11). Judge accuracy on temporal questions +0.314 [0.254, 0.375], positive in all ten conversations.
limits: Single independent author; one benchmark; LLM-judge accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gist or prune steps lose a specific class of detail (dates, numbers, identifiers). Protect those anchors explicitly when summarizing lessons.

source: ZenBrain authors (2026) ZenBrain: a neuroscience-inspired 7-layer memory architecture for autonomous AI systems
finding: Large architecture paper with a sleep consolidation loop and synaptic homeostasis. Headline: the sleep loop adds 37% stability with 47.4% storage reduction.
numbers: Sleep impact measured over 7 simulated days with 350 facts; ablations use a synthetic dataset (300 facts, 100 queries, 45 simulated days at decay 0.15/day). Some components had zero impact under the synthetic stress, per the paper.
limits: Synthetic corpora only; headline numbers are simulation outputs, not task accuracy on real users or benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Treat the headline storage savings as unproven for real tasks.
